name: Wright, Algonquin and Iroquois (MacIntyre Range)

legs.route: Short spur off the main Algonquin trail

legs.connect: Drop back down the spur to the junction, then climb the steep upper trail to the second highest peak in the state.
Follow the short herd path past Boundary Peak, a bump on the ridge, with muddy stretches mostly bridged.

how: All three summits come from one trailhead and one trail. Most parties take the Wright spur first, a very steep slab marked with paint and cairns, then continue to Algonquin and out along the ridge to Iroquois. Some reverse it and pick up Wright on the way down. More than a mile of the route is above treeline, so wind and weather matter. It is steep hiking with scrambling, not roped climbing.
descent: Return over Algonquin to the trailhead on the same trail, or drop through the pass to the lake basin and out through the valley for a loop.
logistics: Day-use and parking fees apply at the lodge; no permit is needed for a day trip. Allow a full day and start early, since the ridge is exposed to wind and storms.
notes: Round trip about 12 miles and 4,300 ft by one page; the other logged 13 miles and about 4,750 ft on a Lake Colden return loop. Prose uses no numbers. One page lists Wright first, the other did Wright spur then Algonquin then Iroquois.

name: Dix Range (Macomb, South Dix, Grace, Hough, Dix)
region: Adirondack High Peaks, Dix Mountain Wilderness

legs.route: Macomb slide from the lean-to cairn

legs.connect: Descend to the col, then climb open rock to the next summit.

legs.route: Out-and-back spur from South Dix (formerly called East Dix)
legs.connect: Follow the herd path nearly a mile each way, through muddy low ground.
Return toward South Dix and continue north along the crest.
Continue on the main ridge trail to the highest summit.

duration: 1 very long day, or 2 days with a lean-to camp
how: Five of the High Peaks sit on one ridge reached from the same trailhead. The usual order starts with the Macomb slide, which is steep loose rock with a bypass to its left, then runs along the ridge to Dix. Many parties do only Macomb, South Dix and Grace as a shorter outing and save Hough and Dix. Mud on the herd paths is deep in wet years, and the exposed summits are a poor place to be in afternoon storms.
descent: A short outing returns by the brook trail from the col below Macomb; the full range ends on a long valley trail or the slide. The slide is slippery when wet, so it is a poor choice for going down.
logistics: Park in the small lot at the end of a gravel road. A lean-to near the slide path suits a two-day split. Fill water at the brook before climbing; none on the summits.
notes: Short version stats from one page: 12.3 miles, 2,279 ft; full range about 15 miles and 5,000 ft by the other. Directions differ (one went Dix first, descending the slide). Both agree on the lean-to start.

name: Mount Coe, South Brother and North Brother loop

legs.route: Marston Trail to the Coe slide trail
Short spur from the trail junction
legs.connect: Follow the narrow ridge, then take the short spur to the summit.
Return to the junction and follow the trail on to the highest of the three; Fort Mountain beyond is a trailless bushwhack.

how: One trailhead serves a loop over all three. The way up Coe is a wide slide of smooth ledges that is risky when wet, with handholds and blazes along its left edge. A narrow ridge leads on to South Brother, with boulder scrambling at the top, and a trail continues to North Brother. Peakbaggers sometimes add Fort Mountain by bushwhack north from North Brother.
descent: Come down the Marston Trail, the gentler trail, rather than the slide.
logistics: Sign in at the park gate; camping needs a reservation. Wet or icy slide rock is the main hazard, so pick a dry day. The slide is harder to follow under snow.
notes: One page logged 11 miles, 4,087 ft; the winter trip did North Brother, Fort, South Brother, then Coe. Direction is reversible. Hamlin Peak pairing not confirmed, omitted.

name: Whiteface and Passaconaway loop

legs.connect: Follow the ridge trail for a couple of miles, then a short spur left to the summit.

how: The loop climbs open ledges to Whiteface, continues over the wooded ridge to Passaconaway, then drops by a gentle valley trail. The ledges are tricky when icy or powdery. Both summits are wooded, with overlooks nearby, and a short spur past Passaconaway gives a wide view.
descent: Descend the valley trail beside a stream for about three miles to the road, a loop instead of an out-and-back.
logistics: Park only in the small lot at the base of the ledge trail; street parking has been ticketed. Several water crossings on the valley trail can be hard at high water or in winter.
notes: One page: about 12 miles and 3,800 ft; search summaries cite 10.3 miles and 2,841 ft (not read). Prose omits numbers.

name: Agassiz and Humphreys (San Francisco Peaks)

legs.route: Up the ski area slopes to the main face
Humphreys Peak Trail along the ridge
legs.connect: Traverse to the saddle between the two, then climb about a mile of gentle ridge on a trail with cairns.

how: Agassiz and Humphreys sit about a mile and a half apart, joined by a broad saddle and a well-trodden ridge. Climbers reach the saddle from the ski area and take Agassiz first, or the reverse. The ridge is icy early in the season and windy. Walking the tundra off-trail is only allowed on snow, to protect rare plants.
descent: Return along the ridge to the saddle, then the ski slopes or the summer trail to the lot.
logistics: Trailhead is at the ski area. Cross-country travel above 11,500 feet is prohibited when snow is not covering the tundra, so stay on the trail outside snow season. Weather shifts quickly; carry layers for wind.
notes: Agassiz summit hiking limited to snow cover per two pages. Humphreys-first order seen in search results only, not read. DROPPED by reviewer: the link itself rests on one trip report.

name: Agassiz and Fremont Peak from Inner Basin

legs.route: Inner Basin Trail to the saddle, then the east slope and north ridge

legs.connect: Return to the saddle, then follow the ridge over a hump; boulder hopping at Class 2.

how: The trail climbs to the saddle below Agassiz, then to the summit by switchbacks and a snow slope. From the saddle a short ridge leads to Fremont. The connecting ridge is easy Class 2, a straightforward traverse. The full range loop also strings these two together with the other peaks on cross-country ground.
descent: Return the way you came by the same ridge and trail; snow slopes may allow a glissade.
logistics: Trailhead is on a forest road that most vehicles reach. Tundra on Agassiz may be hiked only when snow covers it; fines apply otherwise.
notes: One page lists 15.9 miles, 4,800 ft, class 2; the second only confirms Fremont is on the range loop, with straightforward ridge links. DROPPED by reviewer: the link itself rests on one trip report.
